subsidiaryBridges.description: Concrete actual infinities generate metaphysically unacceptable consequences.

sections.title: Causal premise and kinds of beginning
sections.rationale: This exchange contests whether experience and metaphysical intuition about ordinary beginnings justify causation for the universe's absolute beginning.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Whatever begins to exist requires a cause because being cannot arise from non-being without causal powers.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Now since then I have attempted to articulate three arguments in support of the first premise that unpack it a little bit more but still basically rooted in this metaphysical intuition that out of nothing nothing comes and therefore something comes into being there surely has to be a cause that brings it into being.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig asserts metaphysical necessity while primarily supplying intuition rather than an independent demonstration excluding uncaused beginnings.

sections.title: Concrete actual infinities
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether Hilbert-style and Benardete-style consequences are evidence of metaphysical impossibility or merely unfamiliar infinite behavior.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Concrete actual infinities are metaphysically impossible because examples such as Benardete's infinite book produce intolerable concrete consequences despite formal consistency.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If you could have an actual infinite number of things, it would result in all sorts of situations that I think are metaphysically impossible. Granted, there is no strict logical contradiction... the claim is that this is metaphysically impossible... Benardete imagines a book... For there is no last page.

sections.title: Successive formation of an infinite past
sections.rationale: This issue tests the second philosophical route to a finite past: whether a beginningless countdown or temporal series can terminate at the present.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: An actual infinite cannot be formed through successive addition, whether by counting upward from a beginning or downward through a beginningless series to the present.

sourceSpan.excerpt: An actually infinite collection of things, if it were created by God, he'd have to create it all at once... even God couldn't create it by simply adding one book at a time because I think it's impossible for an actual infinite to be formed by successive addition... whether one begins at a point and tries to reach infinity... or one never begins but counts down from infinity to ending at the present.

sections.title: Power of the first cause
sections.rationale: Assuming a first cause, the exchange contests whether the scale and ex nihilo character of the effect warrant attributing enormous causal power.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The first cause is plausibly enormously powerful because it originates a universe ex nihilo, and any proposed chain of intermediate causes must terminate in an absolute creator.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I don't claim that you can show that the creator of the universe is omnipotent or supremely powerful. The word I use is enormously powerful. And the reason for that is because it brings a universe into being out of nothing... this series of demiurges or intermediate causes cannot be infinite in the past. Has to lead back to a first being that is the absolute creator of everything else that follows.

sections.rationale: This final issue directly contests the motion's personal-creator conclusion by comparing agent causation with an impersonal indeterministic alternative.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: A personal explanation is preferable because an eternal impersonal metastable condition with any chance of producing the universe would have produced it from eternity or not at all.

sourceSpan.excerpt: That sort of impersonal indeterministic causation of the universe... We're talking about a non-physical state of affairs and therefore, I think the appropriate category would be a personal explanation because appeal to things like quantum indeterminacy... isn't going to get you the origin of the universe just 13.8 billion years ago... it will either happen from eternity or not at all.

Whether selection for adaptive behavior supplies no reason to expect broadly true beliefs.

response.rationale: Woodford directly answers both the scope inference and the claimed disconnect between evolutionary success and generally accurate representation.

precisionFindings.rationale: He distinguishes atheism from naturalism and broad reliability from perfect access to truth, making the scope of each objection explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is limited to broad truth-tracking and expressly permits systematic mistakes and incomplete access to truth.

charity.alternative: Edwards's strongest argument is that natural selection directly rewards behavior rather than truth, so unguided naturalism lacks a basis for global cognitive trust.
charity.decisiveQualification: Woodford preserves the distinction between perfect truth and broad reliability but argues that false costly representations face selection pressure.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope correction and adaptive truth-tracking answer are distinct, consistent, and directed at the two main inferential steps.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adaptive value of broadly accurate belief is a relevant warrant, but it is asserted generally without evidence about systematic misbelief, abstract cognition, or rival evolutionary models.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts both indispensable components and addresses the inference rather than merely offering unrelated evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con side's central bridge from unguided evolution to untrustworthy cognition.

representationalCharity.rationale: Woodford restates the survival-versus-truth challenge accurately before answering it, with only some rhetorical compression.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The answer separates atheism from naturalism, challenges default inference to theism, and argues that costly false representation is generally selected against.

conMoves.speaker: Simon Edwards
conMoves.proposition: If minds arise through mindless unguided processes selecting advantageous behavior rather than truth, naturalism undercuts confidence in cognition, whereas a rational creator supplies a basis for trustworthy minds.

sourceSpan.excerpt: natural selection does not directly select for True beliefs but rather for advantageous behaviors ... if God exists there is an intelligent Creator ... our minds being rational

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is part of Edwards's uninterrupted prepared opening, introduced by his explicit first argument from rationality.

response.rationale: This is Edwards's initial constructive statement of the argument from reason and evolutionary argument against naturalism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inferential route is recoverable, but atheism, physicalism, naturalism, and unguided evolution are repeatedly treated as interchangeable, and cognitive reliability shifts toward access to truth generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Selection for behavior does not by itself warrant the strong conclusion that naturalistic minds have no reason to trust any belief.

charity.alternative: The strongest naturalistic alternative holds that selection can favor generally accurate representation because successful behavior commonly depends on tracking environmental truths.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument notes that selection acts directly on advantageous behavior but does not address the qualification that truth and fitness can strongly correlate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-defeat route is intelligible, but it moves too quickly from indirect selection for truth to global epistemic distrust.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named philosophical authorities and the behavior-selection premise provide support, but the crucial reliability probabilities and rival model are undeveloped.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive it clearly advances a major affirmative explanation and defines the challenge later debated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The argument directly supports the central con bridge concerning a rational creator and trustworthy cognition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The naturalistic alternative is weakened by omitting the central possibility that accurate representation frequently produces adaptive behavior.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Edwards quotes the argument from reason, distinguishes behavior from truth as evolutionary targets, and contrasts unguided with divinely guided evolution.

sections.title: Fine-tuning, design, and evolutionary explanation
sections.rationale: The con side presents fine-tuning as strong design evidence, while the pro side later argues that developed natural explanations substantially reduce older design-based inferences.

proMoves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
proMoves.proposition: Design inference was more reasonable before evolutionary evidence supplied a detailed natural account of biological complexity; current evidence therefore undercuts broad appeals from complexity or human form to deliberate creation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: before Evolution was put on the board ... it was very hard to look around the world ... Evolution has made it very clear that if God exists he chose to use Evolution

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator has invited both speakers to answer the evolution question, and this continuous portion is distinctly Woodford's response.

components.text: Numerous physical constants allegedly occupy extremely narrow life-permitting ranges.
Those physical constants are alleged to be much more probable under intelligent design than chance.

response.rationale: The move offers issue-bearing naturalistic material about biological complexity, but it does not contact the selected fine-tuning target's physical constants or its comparative likelihood claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The biological-design point is clear, but its relationship to Edwards's distinct cosmic fine-tuning argument remains only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolution strongly explains biological complexity, but it does not by itself settle cosmic fine-tuning or every possible design inference.

charity.alternative: Edwards's strongest design case concerns life-permitting physical constants rather than gaps in biological evolution.
charity.decisiveQualification: Woodford grants that creation belief could once have been rational without a natural account, but his reply does not preserve the cosmological focus.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical and evidential point about biological design is coherent, though its bearing on cosmic fine-tuning is limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolution is a substantial relevant evidential basis for biological complexity, but the span supplies little detail and does not address the cosmological evidence selected in this section.

responsiveness.rationale: It provides relevant contrary design material but contacts neither indispensable component of the earlier physical fine-tuning constructive.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the central natural-explanation bridge by arguing that evolutionary evidence reduces the need for direct biological design inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply treats design broadly and thereby weakens Edwards's more specific physical-constant argument, despite acknowledging a limited historical case.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Woodford contrasts pre-Darwinian design inference with the convergent evidence for evolution and allows that a God, if any, could use evolution.

conMoves.speaker: Simon Edwards
conMoves.proposition: Numerous life-permitting physical constants occupy extremely narrow ranges, making intelligent design far more probable than their occurrence by chance.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the Discovery by physicists that our universe is finely tuned for life ... for all practical intents and purposes impossible ... a super intellect has monkeyed with the physics

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is the explicitly signposted second argument in Edwards's uninterrupted prepared opening.

response.rationale: The move opens Edwards's independent design route and does not answer an earlier selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fine-tuning proposition is clear, but the reference class, probability measure, independence of constants, and alternatives to chance are unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling chance practically impossible and design overwhelmingly probable is disproportionate without a justified probability distribution, independence analysis, or comparison with necessity and selection effects.

charity.alternative: The strongest non-design alternative questions the probability measure over constants and includes necessity, selection effects, or multiple-universe hypotheses rather than simple chance alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: The presentation compares design primarily with undifferentiated chance and does not assess those rival explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood-style inference is intelligible, but the chance calculation and exhaustive comparison of hypotheses are material implicit bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Constants and dramatic numerical analogies are asserted with an authority quotation, but the span supplies no derivation, source detail, independence defense, or rival-hypothesis comparison.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it clearly states and supports an independent cumulative argument for rational theism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the declared central bridge that life-permitting fine-tuning favors intelligent design.

representationalCharity.rationale: The principal alternative is presented as bare chance, omitting stronger necessity, observation-selection, and multiverse formulations.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The argument cites numerous physical parameters, asserts extremely narrow life-permitting values, uses a distant-target analogy, and quotes Fred Hoyle.

sections.title: Objective morality and the Euthyphro dilemma
sections.rationale: The con side treats objective moral value as evidence for God, while the pro side challenges both evolutionary alternatives and the coherence of identifying divine character with goodness.

proMoves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
proMoves.proposition: Evolution of cooperative social groups explains moral intuitions and persistent disagreement under either atheism or theism, so those intuitions do not uniquely support an objective divine moral law.

sourceSpan.excerpt: under a theist or an atheistic view evolution provides a very simple explanation for the moral feelings that we have ... explains why there's so much moral disagreement

proMoves.attributionBasis: This is Woodford's continuous response to Edwards's challenge about moral normativity and the way the world should be.

components.text: Shared intuitions about serious wrongs are evidence of an objective moral law.
The cited wrongs remain objectively wrong rather than merely disfavored evolved responses.
Impersonal reality cannot ground genuine obligation, making God the best explanation.

response.rationale: The reply gives an evolutionary explanation for moral intuitions and disagreement, thereby weakening their uniqueness as theistic evidence, but it does not answer whether objective obligations exist or require grounding.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolutionary explanation of moral feelings and disagreement is recoverable, but its reach sometimes slides from explaining intuitions to suggesting difficulty for an objective moral framework generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Social selection plausibly explains some cooperative intuitions and disagreement, but the move gives limited support for extending that explanation across the full range of moral cognition.

charity.alternative: Edwards's strongest claim is ontological: objective wrongness requires a transcendent personal ground, not merely a causal account of moral feelings.
charity.decisiveQualification: Woodford supplies a causal genealogy and disagreement evidence but does not claim that these alone ground objective obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply coherently offers a nonunique cause of moral feelings and disagreement, but explaining belief formation does not by itself settle the truth or grounding of moral propositions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The social-cooperation mechanism is relevant and intelligible, but it is presented schematically without evidence sufficient to explain diverse moral judgments or objective normativity.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the appeal from intuition by supplying a rival genealogy, but leaves the decisive objectivity and metaphysical-grounding components unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially attacks the central divine-grounding bridge by offering a rival account of its principal observed evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: Woodford explicitly formulates the evolutionary account as compatible with theism, avoiding the weaker claim that evolution alone disproves God.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The span describes differential survival of cooperative groups and connects that process to moral sentiments and disagreement over sex and gender norms.

proMoves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
proMoves.proposition: Saying that God is goodness merely relocates the Euthyphro dilemma: either divine character aligns with an independent good or divine character defines good and remains arbitrary.

sourceSpan.excerpt: it's just kicking the can down the road ... is God good because what he aligns with is some goodness ... or is he good because he defines what good is

proMoves.attributionBasis: Edwards has just completed his God-is-the-good answer, and the transcript clearly marks Woodford's immediate rejoinder.

components.text: Whether identifying God with goodness supplies a non-arbitrary grounding rather than restating the disputed identity.

response.rationale: Woodford diagnoses the asserted identity as question-begging and explicitly states the defeating consequence that both original horns remain.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reformulated dilemma, its two horns, and the claimed consequence for Edwards's answer are all explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that the dilemma succeeds does not engage the strongest necessary-nature account, so its defeating force exceeds the conceptual work supplied.

charity.alternative: Edwards's strongest answer identifies goodness with God's necessary character rather than with commands or an external abstract standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: Woodford preserves that identity claim but argues it still requires an account of why the character merits the term good.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reapplying the dilemma to divine character is intelligible and exposes an explanatory demand, but it assumes rather than demonstrates that the third option collapses into a horn.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: As a conceptual rejoinder it needs little empirical evidence, yet it supplies no developed modal or metaethical warrant for excluding a necessary-character identity.

responsiveness.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive character-based answer, diagnoses relocation as the defect, and explicitly states why that defect allegedly leaves the dilemma undefeated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central bridge grounding objective morality in God's character.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately identifies the character-based proposal, but treats it as simple definitional arbitrariness without engaging its strongest necessary-nature qualification.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The immediate rejoinder repeats the God-is-good proposal in its strongest form and asks whether goodness is prior to or constituted by that nature.

conMoves.speaker: Simon Edwards
conMoves.proposition: Objective wrongs such as racism, bullying, and sexual abuse are best explained by an objective moral law grounded in God, because impersonal physical reality cannot itself generate obligations.

sourceSpan.excerpt: some things such as bullying or racism or sexual abuse are objectively wrong ... the existence of this objective moral law points us to the existence of God

conMoves.attributionBasis: This is the explicitly signposted third argument in Edwards's continuous prepared opening.

response.rationale: This is the first selected statement of Edwards's moral argument and therefore has no preceding response target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objective-law and divine-grounding claims are clear, though the exact kind of objectivity and dependence relation are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move treats God as the only good explanation, but does not eliminate secular moral realism or show why objective reasons require a personal lawgiver.

charity.alternative: The strongest secular alternative accepts objective moral truths while grounding them in non-theistic normative facts rather than opinions or physical particles having attitudes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Edwards mentions non-theistic objective morality but characterizes its ground mainly through an impersonal-particles contrast.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is clear, but the move from impersonal reality to the impossibility of objective normative facts remains an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete moral examples and philosophical references establish intuitive appeal, but intuition and authority do not substantiate the claimed exclusivity of divine grounding.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it establishes a clear independent component of the cumulative affirmative case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central con bridge that objective morality is best grounded in a personal creator.

representationalCharity.rationale: The secular realist alternative is compressed into impersonal particles having opinions, which does not capture its strongest normative account.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Edwards invokes apparently objective wrongs, argues that denial conflicts with deep intuitions, and claims an impersonal universe cannot ground moral law.

conMoves.speaker: Simon Edwards
conMoves.proposition: The Euthyphro dilemma is false because God neither follows an external good nor arbitrarily invents goodness; God's character is itself the personal source of objective goodness.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the answer to the Euthyphro dilemma ... God commands what he does not because it is good but because he is the good ... ultimately sourced in the person of God

conMoves.attributionBasis: Woodford explicitly poses the dilemma and Edwards immediately identifies and answers it in this uninterrupted span.

components.text: Evolution provides a nonunique explanation of moral feelings under both theism and atheism.
Persistent moral disagreement weakens the inference to a clear objective divine moral law.

response.rationale: Although this turn answers an intervening Euthyphro objection in the complete transcript, it does not contact either component of the earlier locked pro-moral-evolution move and instead supplies relevant contrary grounding material.

precisionFindings.rationale: The third-option identity claim is clearly stated, although the metaphysical meaning of God being identical with goodness remains compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposal is a coherent candidate ground, but the assertion that only the creator can qualify as goodness's source is not independently established.

charity.alternative: Woodford's stronger alternative explains moral intuitions evolutionarily and challenges whether divine grounding avoids arbitrariness or dependence on an external standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: Edwards answers the grounding demand through God's nature but does not yet address the reformulated arbitrariness challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The nature-based third option coherently avoids simple command voluntarism, though the identity between God and goodness requires further argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The answer accurately states both horns and offers an intuitive personal ground, but provides no independent warrant for the crucial identity or necessity claim.

responsiveness.rationale: Relative to the preceding locked pro target, it supplies issue-bearing moral material but contacts none of the evolutionary-genealogy or disagreement components.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The answer directly supports the central con morality bridge at the point of its principal conceptual challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The two horns of the Euthyphro dilemma are stated accurately and at their strongest before the character-based alternative is proposed.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Edwards accurately states both traditional horns and proposes the standard divine-nature response, linking moral experience to a personal ultimate source.

sections.title: Salvation confusion and revelation
sections.rationale: The pro side argues that culturally variable, disputed revelation is incompatible with high-stakes salvation requirements, while both sides address how scriptural claims should be evaluated.

proMoves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
proMoves.proposition: An all-loving God would not attach grave postmortem consequences to accepting disputed propositions when religious communities disagree about salvation and the supposed evidential hoop is difficult to identify.

sourceSpan.excerpt: most Christians let alone Muslims and Jews can't even agree on what's necessary for salvation ... those of us ... who cannot see the hoop ... be eternally punished

proMoves.attributionBasis: This span is the concluding argument of Woodford's uninterrupted prepared opening immediately before the moderator thanks him.

response.rationale: This is Woodford's opening salvation-confusion argument and has no earlier selected argumentative target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The salvation-confusion proposition is recoverable and universalism is acknowledged, but claims about most theists, required beliefs, and postmortem consequences range across materially different traditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move culminates in categorical declarations of absurdity and irrationality, while its broad doctrinal and demographic premises receive assertion rather than adequate support.

charity.alternative: The strongest theistic alternative permits inclusivism, universalism, genre-sensitive revelation, or judgment proportioned to access rather than explicit doctrinal assent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Woodford acknowledges universalism but describes it as fringe and focuses on prevalent exclusivist or annihilationist views.

logicalCoherence.rationale: There is a clear tension between loving disclosure, grave stakes, and doctrinal confusion, but the conclusion generalizes beyond the punitive salvation models actually described.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Real interreligious disagreement is identified, yet prevalence, doctrinal requirements, cultural dependence, and the marginality of universalism are asserted without supporting detail.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly advances an independent route against the rationality of the specified God belief.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro bridge concerning confused high-stakes revelation and salvation requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges universalism and variation in required propositions, but treats a broad punitive model as representative of the vast majority without sufficient qualification.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Woodford lists doctrinal propositions associated with salvation, contrasts annihilation and eternal torment, notes universalism, and emphasizes disagreement across and within religions.

proMoves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
proMoves.proposition: Some biblical history may be credible, but historical existence does not establish resurrection or miracles, and an all-loving God would not require belief in claims that largely track cultural upbringing.

sourceSpan.excerpt: some of the stories in the Bible are true but plenty of them are not ... it's a mistake to think that because he existed he resurrected ... born and bred to take it seriously

proMoves.attributionBasis: After Edwards answers the audience question about biblical stories, the moderator explicitly invites Woodford's answer and he speaks continuously.

components.text: The Bible contains historical records, poetry, parables, and other distinct literary genres.
Accepting biblical revelation need not involve treating every narrated story as literal history.

response.rationale: Woodford supplies relevant contrary material about historical inference, miracles, and cultural uptake, but neither disputes the existence of multiple genres nor answers the compatibility claim made by the selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: He carefully distinguishes historical existence from supernatural claims and explicitly says only some stories are false.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The existence-versus-resurrection distinction is well calibrated, but the categorical dismissal of miracles and cultural rationality rests on unsupported consensus and upbringing claims.

charity.alternative: Edwards's strongest position is that the Bible contains multiple genres and can preserve genuine history while treating parables and poetry nonliterally.
charity.decisiveQualification: Woodford grants that some biblical claims and Jesus's existence are historically credible but separates those concessions from miracle claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference-blocking distinction between a person's existence and attributed miracles is clear and consistently applied across religions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scholarly consensus and cultural upbringing are invoked without detail, while the core point that ordinary historical existence does not entail resurrection is well warranted.

responsiveness.rationale: The material concerns scripture and belief but leaves both indispensable genre components uncontacted, placing it in the relevant-nonanswer band.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the central revelation bridge by challenging miracle inference and arguing that serious religious belief tracks cultural upbringing.

representationalCharity.rationale: Woodford explicitly grants historical content and Jesus's probable existence before denying that these concessions establish miraculous claims.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The reply distinguishes history from miracle attribution, compares Christian and Islamic claims, and links confidence in revelation to cultural formation.

conMoves.speaker: Simon Edwards
conMoves.proposition: Human beings exist intentionally because God wanted them, and divine purpose is compatible with God using guided evolutionary mechanisms rather than direct creation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: we're here on purpose because somebody God wanted us to be here ... hugely open to the idea that God could have used mechanisms of natural selection ... guided Evolution

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the audience's human-origins question to Edwards, who gives this continuous answer before Woodford begins.

response.rationale: The answer independently advances the con route's guided-evolution subsidiary bridge rather than replying to an earlier selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: Purpose and guided evolution are clear, though the distinction between evolutionary mechanism and divine guidance is not operationally specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Edwards expressly remains open and uncertain about evolutionary scope, but the assertion of intended human purpose is not independently warranted here.

charity.alternative: The strongest evolutionary alternative accepts nonrandom natural selection while denying that the process intended the arrival of particular persons or humanity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Edwards accepts natural selection as a possible mechanism but adds purposive divine guidance at the explanatory level.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Guidance and evolutionary mechanism are logically compatible, although compatibility alone does not establish that guidance occurred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The purpose claim is unsupported, and references to literature, mathematics, and explanatory difficulties remain nonspecific despite appropriate acknowledgment of uncertainty.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive it usefully clarifies that the con route need not reject evolution, though it only partly bears on revelation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the declared subsidiary guided-evolution bridge rather than the complete motion-level case.

representationalCharity.rationale: Edwards accepts substantial explanatory work by evolution and does not portray acceptance of natural selection as necessarily atheistic.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Edwards distinguishes purposive origin from mechanism, accepts possible guided evolution, and expresses uncertainty about whether macroevolution explains everything.

conMoves.speaker: Simon Edwards
conMoves.proposition: Rational interpretation of the Bible distinguishes historical records, poetry, and parables, so accepting biblical revelation does not require treating every narrated story as literal history.

sourceSpan.excerpt: it's a collection of different books and some books are clearly historical records ... some books are poetry ... they were stories, parables

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the audience's Bible question to Edwards, and he answers continuously until inviting Woodford to add his view.

response.rationale: Although late in the debate, this is Edwards's first selected statement of the genre-sensitive revelation claim and targets the audience question rather than a selected move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response clearly distinguishes genres and gives parables as explicit examples of nonhistorical narrative.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest interpretive claim follows from the stated diversity of biblical genres and does not assert that every historical or miraculous claim is established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence ratings (86 and 84), whose difference remained below every dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Good Samaritan and prodigal son illustrate the distinction effectively, though the span does not provide criteria for classifying disputed passages.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it supplies a competent but limited interpretive principle rather than a complete defense of biblical revelation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The adjudicated ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed relevanceBurden ratings (72 and 70), whose difference remained below every dispute trigger.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not represent or attack a live selected alternative, so charity is untested under the fixed anchor.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Edwards identifies the Bible as a collection of genres and uses Jesus's parables to distinguish a story's teaching role from literal historical occurrence.

routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the best cumulative explanation of cosmological, fine-tuning, moral, historical, and experiential evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the principal evidence families materially favor a personal, morally good creator revealed through Jesus over skeptical atheism.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative evidence makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: The universe began and therefore has a transcendent personal cause.
Life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than necessity or chance.
Objective moral values and duties exist and require God as their ontological ground.
The principal historical facts concerning Jesus are best explained by his resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Sincere immediate experience can provide properly basic awareness of God.
A timeless immaterial cause is more plausibly an unembodied mind than an abstract object.

routes.description: Show that Craig's evidence is too uncertain, underdetermining, or naturally explicable to justify the specific Christian God hypothesis.
routes.successCriteria: Defeat enough indispensable evidential bridges that skeptical atheism remains more reasonable than accepting the specific Christian God hypothesis.

motionBridge.description: The presented evidence does not justify preferring Christian theism to skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Cosmological evidence and causal intuitions underdetermine a beginning, transcendent cause, or mind.
Fine-tuning probabilities and designer inferences are premature and do not identify the Christian God.
Moral realism and intrinsic value are available without positing a divine ontological ground.
Dependent late religious sources and ordinary psychology weaken the resurrection inference.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Conflicting culturally transmitted religions undermine religious experience as a reliable method.
Sincere nonbelief and unclear evidence count against the proposed loving, relationship-seeking God.

sections.title: Cosmic beginning, causation, and a personal cause
sections.rationale: This sustained exchange tests the beginning premise, causal principle, and inference from a nonphysical cause to an unembodied mind.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: A finite cosmic past and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin result support an absolute beginning, which requires a transcendent immaterial personal cause.

sourceSpan.excerpt: past events must be finite in number; therefore the universe began to exist and has a transcendent cause

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs continuously within Craig's identified opening presentation and follows his announced first argument.

response.rationale: This is Craig's initial affirmative cosmological case and therefore has no earlier selected argumentative target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogistic route is explicit, but the transitions among local universe, global universe, spacetime boundary, and absolute beginning remain partly compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Craig acknowledges the missing quantum-gravity description but still treats the theorem, causal principle, and mind-versus-abstract-object disjunction as necessitating a personal creator.

charity.alternative: A past-eternal or physically prior cosmology may evade an absolute beginning, and a nonphysical cause need not be either an abstract object or a mind.
charity.decisiveQualification: The strongest alternative accepts present cosmological evidence while denying that it establishes a global beginning or exhausts the possible kinds of cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explicit core syllogism is valid, but the actual-infinity argument, global scope transition, and exhaustive abstract-object-or-mind disjunction leave material inferential bridges unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names a theorem and relevant cosmological considerations, yet its interpretation and the metaphysical causal and personal-cause conclusions receive substantially less support than their asserted force requires.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it presents a sustained and intelligible route through the beginning, causal, transcendent, and personal-cause claims without relying on an invented prior target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the declared central cosmology bridge and is rated within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: It identifies eternal cosmologies and nonpersonal alternatives, but dismisses speculative models collectively and frames the causal candidates too narrowly for the strongest skeptical alternative.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 155–251 contain the finite-past argument, BGV appeal, causal syllogism, divine-attribute derivation, and mind-versus-abstract-object inference.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Experience does not license creation-ex-nihilo causation, current cosmology does not establish an absolute global beginning, and a nonphysical cause need not be a mind.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I cannot infer from my own experience that creation from nothing is causal in the same way; the theorem proves less than Bill needs

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is within Millican's identified opening case and explicitly introduces and criticizes Craig's Kalam premises.

components.text: The global universe had an absolute temporal beginning.
Whatever begins ex nihilo must have a transcendent cause.
The nonphysical cause must be an unembodied mind.

response.rationale: Millican separately challenges the absolute-beginning evidence, the extrapolation of causation to creation ex nihilo, and the restricted inference to an unembodied mind.

precisionFindings.rationale: Millican explicitly distinguishes local from global universe and separates the causal, temporal, and mental-substance objections.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He frames the conclusion as doubt and underdetermination, repeatedly emphasizing the limitations of current physics and human experience.

charity.alternative: Craig's strongest case combines a philosophical finite-past argument, BGV cosmology, a causal principle, and elimination of nonmental candidates.
charity.decisiveQualification: BGV concerns average expansion and does not by itself exclude every prior contracting or unknown physical regime.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply consistently separates the premises and shows why each inferential extension requires additional support.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies concrete cosmological distinctions, a theorem quotation, model alternatives, and mind-body evidence, with residual gaps concerning the vacuum and the exact status of proposed cosmologies.

responsiveness.rationale: The response directly contacts all three indispensable stages of the selected cosmological case and explicitly explains why each stage fails to compel the personal-cause conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central cosmology bridge and is rated within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican reconstructs the valid Kalam form and distinguishes its stages before disputing its premises, with only minor compression of Craig's modal defense.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 775–973 present the Kalam form, objections from causal experience, composition, local/global cosmology, BGV limitations, and the unsupported-mind objection.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Life-permitting constants and initial conditions display extreme improbability plus an independent pattern, favoring design over necessity or chance.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are only three possible explanations of this extraordinary fine-tuning: physical necessity, chance, or design

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly labels fine-tuning as his second opening argument and delivers this uninterrupted inference.

response.rationale: This is the first selected statement of Craig's design argument and has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory trilemma is recoverable, but the probability space and scope of physical necessity are not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident elimination of chance and necessity exceeds the supplied specification of possible values, priors, and rival cosmological explanations.

charity.alternative: Chance may operate through observer selection or multiple universes, while apparent parameter freedom may be reduced by deeper physical laws not yet known.
charity.decisiveQualification: The strongest nondesign alternative does not treat the constants as a single unconditioned random draw from a known uniform probability distribution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but the trilemma is insufficiently defended and the move passes from improbability plus a pattern to design without establishing the relevant probability model.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It describes constants, initial conditions, and life-permitting sensitivity, but supplies no quantitative distribution and gives compressed treatment to necessity, chance, and observer-selection alternatives.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive it clearly lays out the phenomenon, candidate explanations, and intended design conclusion, with no earlier locked response obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the declared central fine-tuning bridge and stays within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Necessity and chance are named, but the strongest chance and deeper-law versions are compressed into a simple trilemma, weakening the alternatives on which the design inference depends.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 286–321 state the necessity-chance-design trilemma, patterned-improbability warrant, and designer conclusion.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Fine-tuning is intriguing but present physics and probability assignments are too immature, while the data neither establish moral perfection nor fit uniquely with an omnipotent Christian creator.

sourceSpan.excerpt: a physically inexplicable coincidence would invite a cosmic designer, but I also see good reason for caution and modesty

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican is explicitly reintroduced for this rebuttal and announces that he is addressing the fine-tuning argument.

charity.decisiveQualification: That conditional inference would establish at most a powerful designer unless further evidence identified moral perfection and specifically Christian attributes.

sections.title: Objective morality and divine grounding
sections.rationale: The speakers contest both the existence and interpretation of objective moral facts and whether their ontological ground must be divine.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist, while atheistic evolution and conditioning cannot make them objectively binding; therefore God exists as their ground.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if God did not exist objective moral values and duties would not exist; objective moral values and duties do exist

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig announces this as his third argument during his uninterrupted opening statement.

response.rationale: This is the initial selected formulation of Craig's moral argument and therefore has no earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism and belief-independent definition are clear, but objective value, duty, bindingness, and ontological grounding are not fully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The deductive conclusion depends on a controversial grounding premise supported mainly by evolutionary genealogy and selected testimony rather than elimination of secular realism.

charity.alternative: Atheistic naturalism can explain moral belief and cooperative conduct through evolution and social conditioning.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explaining the origin of moral belief does not by itself settle whether secular objective moral truths or reasons exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated modus-tollens structure is valid, but the move shifts too quickly from naturalistic genealogy to the impossibility of secular normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral experience and quotations supply relevant material, but selective reliance on an evolutionary anti-realist does not establish what atheism or nontheistic moral realism must entail.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly advances Craig's moral route and requires no earlier selected response.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the pro route's central morality bridge and is scored within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move largely represents the nontheistic alternative as evolutionary herd morality, omitting stronger realist accounts whose distinction from moral psychology is decisive to the argument.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 322–400 define objective morality, give an evolutionary genealogy, appeal to moral apprehension, and infer God from the two premises.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Many nontheists are moral realists, and neither moral perception nor human intrinsic value becomes intelligible only by adding an undetected divine ground.

sourceSpan.excerpt: 56.3 percent were moral realists but only 14.6 percent were theists, so there are plenty of moral realists who are not theists

conMoves.attributionBasis: The chair has returned the floor to Millican, who explicitly identifies moral realism as the issue under discussion.

components.text: Objective moral values and duties exist as more than evolved social conditioning.
Atheism cannot accommodate intrinsic value or objectively binding moral reasons.
God's existence is required as the ontological ground of objective morality.

response.rationale: Millican accepts the live possibility of moral realism, challenges the denial of nontheistic intrinsic value, and directly questions how an undetected God supplies the alleged ontological ground.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding objection is clear, though Millican openly notes that the word objective bundles several meanings he has not fully resolved.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He presents the survey as pressure against Craig's premise rather than proof and admits difficulty giving a universally persuasive account of value.

charity.alternative: Craig distinguishes atheists' ability to know moral truths from the ontological question of what makes those truths objectively binding.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that nontheists believe moral realism does not by itself supply the ontology Craig demands.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between moral knowledge and ontology is recognized, but the survey and examples establish conceptual availability more readily than a complete nontheistic ground.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant ratings (73 and 71), whose difference remained below every dispute trigger.

responsiveness.rationale: The move contacts the existence, nontheistic-grounding, and divine-grounding components, directly engaging the strongest ontological form rather than only moral knowledge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The adjudicated ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed relevanceBurden ratings (86 and 84), whose difference remained below every dispute trigger.

sections.title: Resurrection evidence and natural explanation
sections.rationale: This issue tests the specifically Christian bridge: whether the historical sources establish facts whose best explanation is a divine resurrection.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples' unexpected resurrection belief are widely accepted facts best explained by Jesus rising from the dead.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are actually three facts recognized by the majority of historians today which I believe are best explained by the resurrection

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his fourth opening argument and enumerates the three historical claims in a continuous span.

response.rationale: This is Craig's first selected historical argument and therefore has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three facts and conclusion are clear, but the scope of scholarly consensus and the comparative class of natural explanations remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that no plausible naturalistic explanation exists is much stronger than the brief consensus citations and dismissal of two alternatives establish.

charity.alternative: Natural explanations include body removal, survival, legendary development, visionary experience, and psychological reinforcement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting selected older alternatives does not exhaust combinations of source dependence, memory, legend, and religious psychology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Inference to a resurrection from the three stated facts is intelligible, but the move treats rejection of two alternatives as if it exhausted the natural explanatory field.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 426–470 enumerate the empty tomb, appearances, and transformed belief, cite scholarly opinions, reject two alternatives, and infer resurrection.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: The Gospel accounts are late, interested, mutually dependent, discrepant, and poorly corroborated, so they provide weak grounds for overturning ordinary natural explanations.

sourceSpan.excerpt: four accounts all written many years after the alleged events, not by eyewitnesses but by devoted Christians

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly announces that he is turning to the resurrection and delivers the source criticism continuously.

components.text: The three asserted facts have sufficiently strong independent historical attestation.
A literal resurrection explains the evidence better than natural historical development.

response.rationale: Millican attacks the evidential foundation through dating, authorship, dependence, discrepancies, selection, and absent corroboration, thereby challenging both the facts and miracle inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-critical proposition and its intended evidential consequence are explicit and consistently bounded to the available Gospel accounts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The criticisms warrant substantial caution, though several historical claims are asserted rapidly and do not fully analyze Craig's non-Gospel traditions.

charity.alternative: Craig's minimal-facts case relies on claims of broad scholarly acceptance rather than treating every Gospel detail as equally reliable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Discrepancies in secondary details do not automatically defeat the empty tomb, experiences, or subsequent belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The connection from dependent, interested, discrepant sources to reduced evidential force is coherent, with a bounded gap concerning minimal facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete dependence and corroboration issues support skepticism, though the treatment of dating and all relevant traditions is compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The reply contacts both the factual foundation and best-explanation inference of Craig's selected historical case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the pro route's central resurrection bridge and is scored within the central tier band.

representationalCharity.rationale: Millican engages the historical evidence directly but partially conflates criticism of full narratives with Craig's narrower minimal-facts formulation.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 2056–2110 discuss late non-eyewitness authorship, Synoptic dependence, discrepancies, canonical selection, and lack of external corroboration.

sections.title: Religious experience, diversity, and hiddenness
sections.rationale: The final contested family concerns whether immediate experience reliably reveals God despite conflicting religions and sincere, reflective nonbelief.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: God can be known immediately apart from argument, and sincere seekers who draw near to God will encounter an evident divine reality.

sourceSpan.excerpt: you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments simply by immediately experiencing him

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig labels personal experience as his fifth consideration in the same identified opening speech.

response.rationale: This is the initial selected experiential claim, offered before Millican's diversity and sincere-seeker objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: Immediate experience is identifiable, but sincere seeking, divine self-disclosure, and the scope of the universal-seeming promise are not operationally delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal assurance to sincere seekers rests on scriptural promise and reported experience without addressing conflicting or absent experiences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move supplies an intelligible experiential route, but it does not bridge from felt immediacy to knowledge or make the universal sincere-seeker promise resistant to counterexample.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A quotation describing biblical experience and a scriptural promise illustrate the claim but provide little independent warrant for its reliability or universal seeker condition.

responsiveness.rationale: The adjudicated ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed responsiveness ratings (80 and 77), whose difference remained below every dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The adjudicated ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed relevanceBurden ratings (68 and 70), whose difference remained below every dispute trigger.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 471–505 distinguish immediate experience from argument, cite John Hick and scripture, and promise disclosure to sincere seekers.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Conflicting culturally acquired religions make religious experience unreliable, while his own prolonged sincere inquiry ending in nonbelief directly challenges promised disclosure.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if some method of acquiring beliefs leads to lots of different and conflicting beliefs, then that method cannot be relied on

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Millican's identified opening presentation and expressly anticipates and rejects the genetic-fallacy interpretation.

components.text: Immediate religious experience can itself provide reliable knowledge of God.
Every sincere seeker will receive evident personal disclosure from God.

response.rationale: The diversity argument directly challenges the reliability of religious experience, but this locked span does not present Millican's personal sincere-inquiry counterexample to the promised disclosure claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: Millican carefully states that dubious origins do not prove falsity and limits his conclusion to the unreliability of the shared belief-forming methods.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He argues for reduced reliability and a strong burden rather than claiming that diversity deductively disproves Christianity.

charity.alternative: Craig combines immediate experience with logic and public evidence rather than relying solely on inherited religious belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Diversity directly undermines experiential method only to the extent that incompatible traditions use materially similar experiences and transmission processes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument identifies a genuine reliability problem, but it moves too quickly from diverse conflicting beliefs to a categorical verdict about several grouped methods.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Geographic transmission and religious conflict provide relevant support, but the span offers no comparative reliability evidence and overuses the contrast with scientific practice.

responsiveness.rationale: The move contacts the decisive reliability component of Craig's experience claim but leaves the sincere-seeker disclosure component untouched within the locked source span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the declared subsidiary experience bridge and is rated at the top of the subsidiary tier band.
